title: A plan of return
hookLine: what the laws of return ask of your life right now
tomorrow: the laws began with confession. how do they end?

cards: Sunday, after the last show. The set is struck, the costumes are bagged, and the group chat is all photos and inside jokes. Somebody's mom asks the classic question: so, what did you learn?
Here's a less classic one. These laws of return have walked from confession to love. What would they look like written down as a plan, for one real thing in your life?

teach.h: ONE: NAME IT AND LEAVE IT.
teach.b: Gather what the laws have said, and the plan almost writes itself. Step one: name it and leave it. Chapter two: leave the wrong, put it out of your thoughts, regret it, resolve not to go back.
And chapter seven adds: if it's a trait, the anger or the envy, name that too.

teach.h: TWO: SAY IT AND REPAIR IT.
teach.b: Step two: say it, and repair it. Chapter one: teshuvah includes words, said out loud.
Chapter two: if you wronged a person, Yom Kippur doesn't clear it until you've made it right with them; ask, and if you're refused, ask again. Step three: meet the moment again.
Complete return, Maimonides says, is when the same chance comes back, you could do it again, and you choose not to. That's the test, and it can't be rushed.

teach.h: NOT FAR. LET THEM BE NEW.
teach.b: It arrives on the calendar of your life, not of your feelings. And underneath the three steps, the posture of the later chapters: don't count yourself far. Let other people be new.
Grow slowly, from reward toward love.
Here's what's worth telling a friend: in this law book, a plan of return isn't a punishment schedule. It's a way home with the turns marked.

how: In the month of Elul, before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally make a personal accounting, cheshbon ha-nefesh, and set out concrete steps of teshuvah, including asking forgiveness from people they've wronged.

games.q: what does “a plan of return” mean?
o: a single confession that wipes the slate clean
a schedule of punishments for what you have done
steps toward changing: name, repair, choose again

games.q: which chapter gives which step — tap the pairs.
p: traits too; don't count yourself far

s: return is finished once you feel sorry
regret is one step; leaving it, saying it, repairing and the same chance come too.
for wrongs against people, Yom Kippur alone doesn't clear them
Maimonides: not until you've made it right with them.
complete return means you never face that temptation again
it means facing the same chance and choosing differently.

games.q: a friend vows to stop gossiping, and for a month there's simply nothing to gossip about. is her return complete?
o: not yet; complete return comes when the same chance returns and she chooses differently.
yes; a whole month without gossip is complete return.
yes; the vow itself, said out loud, completes it.
games.why: Maimonides' complete return needs the same chance: able to do it again, and choosing not to. a quiet month is a good start, not the test.

practice: Pick one thing you'd like to return from: a habit, a trait, a strained friendship. Name the wish in a few words, then the moment most likely to trip you, then one if-then: if that moment comes, then I'll do this instead.
Say the if-then to yourself until it's easy to remember, and rest with it for the time that's left.

wordCard.voice: A plan of return: name it and leave it, say it and repair it, then meet the same chance and choose differently.

orig.note: Hebrew: return; from shuv, to turn back.

carryVoice: To keep close: a plan to return, and the third step waits for the moment. Twenty-nine of thirty, one to go.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 1:1 (return includes spoken confession)
Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 2:1–2 (complete return: the same chance, able, and choosing not to; leave, regret, resolve)
Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 2:9 (Yom Kippur does not atone for wrongs against others until they are appeased; ask again if refused)
Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 7:3–4, 7:8, 10:5 (traits; don't count yourself far; don't remind returners; slowly toward love)
